A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Generation from Noisy Examples. All 19 pages of v1 and 15 pages of v2, including their appendices, support comparison; definitions and proofs can be matched across renaming and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports mathematical definitions, algorithms, theorems, proofs, and counterexamples, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

after.justification: v2 remains entirely theoretical, including Appendices A–G. Its added LLM motivation cites other work rather than reporting original empirical results.

M1.justification: Appendices E–F restrict generator index searches to {1,...,t}, whereas v1 maximizes over all natural numbers. Algorithm 1 changes its loop endpoint from r_t to r_t-1 and its fallback output from candidate r_t+1 to r_t. Appendix C also supplies a related closure-based generator. These are procedural additions and corrections within the retained approach.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or empirical training/evaluation tasks. The added discussion of training LLMs on generated outputs is motivation, not evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates empirical comparison methods or baselines. Comparisons with earlier work concern theoretical guarantees.

E3.justification: Neither version contains experimental protocols, splits, evaluation metrics, or training budgets. Revisions to theoretical sample thresholds belong under T1.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, sensitivity experiments, robustness tests, or empirical case studies. Noise tolerance is studied through mathematical arguments.

E5.justification: Repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, and statistical uncertainty estimates are absent from both versions.

E6.justification: Neither version reports empirical scores, rankings, or qualitative experimental findings. Changes to mathematical results and guarantees are assessed under T1.

T1.justification: v1 Definition 2.5 counts distinct positive examples; v2 retains it as Definition C.1 but introduces total-example counting in Definition 2.4 and replaces Theorem 3.1's proof. Appendix C restricts the earlier proof argument to an explicit subclass condition in Lemma C.2 and adds the characterization sup_n(NC_n(H)-n) < infinity with a proof sketch. Appendices E–F revise sufficient sample bounds to accommodate bounded index searches, and Algorithm 1's proof receives indexing corrections. Appendix G also drops v1's explicit late-noise cutoff from its final guarantee.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal noise-dependent and countable-class contributions are retained. However, introduction contribution (4)'s finite-union sufficiency claim now invokes the stronger total-example noise-independent notion; v1's corresponding premise used positive-example counting. This narrows that stated sufficient condition beyond merely renaming it.

C2.justification: Section 3.2 adds a quantitative sample-complexity interpretation of the Noisy Closure dimension and changes the comparison with learning theory to emphasize deterministic online learning. Section 4 removes v1's Questions 4.3–4.4 and their discussion of possible noisy/noiseless separations requiring uncountable classes. The information-theoretic scope and unresolved characterization/computability questions remain.

D1.justification: Neither version supplies implementation environments, hardware, experimental hyperparameters, runtime measurements, or code/data access information. The revised mathematical generator constructions are covered under M1 and T1.

R1.justification: v2 adds Burns et al. (2023) and Briesch et al. (2023) to motivate noisy training on LLM outputs. It also revises the relationship to online-learning results, replacing v1's broad equivalence comparison with a distinction for deterministic algorithms. The central positioning relative to Kleinberg and Mullainathan and Li et al. remains.

P1.justification: v2 systematically replaces the easily confused noisy/uniform terminology with noise-dependent and noise-independent terminology. It moves noiseless definitions and background results into Appendices A–B and several proofs into E–G, replacing them with main-text summaries. It also shortens the discussion and adds acknowledgements and an impact statement, substantially reorganizing the narrative.

P2.justification: The single-column manuscript becomes a two-column conference paper for the main text and references, with single-column appendices. Typography, headers, author information, and equation wrapping change throughout. Algorithm 1 is reformatted into a narrow column without its previous line numbering. Neither version contains empirical figures or tables.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important theoretical defect: v1's Theorem 3.1 relied on an unjustified minimal-subclass step for positive-example counting. v2 separates total-count and positive-count guarantees, replaces the main proof, and supplies a separate characterization in Appendix C. Bounded index searches in Appendices E–F also repair generator definitions. Incorrect Appendix C cross-references and Appendix G's dropped late-noise cutoff remain weaknesses, but the central mathematical corrections provide a substantial net improvement.
